title: Service Discovery
subtitle: Watch an Orders service find, health-check and call a Payments service whose instances keep changing addresses.
learn: Why hard-coded addresses break when instances autoscale, crash and redeploy
How registration, heartbeats and TTLs keep a registry honest
The difference between client-side and server-side discovery, and what each costs
How DNS-based discovery works and why caching makes it sluggish
What happens to callers during the stale window after an instance dies

steps.title: Where is Payments right now?
steps.body: Orders must call Payments. In a fixed setup you would write Payments' address into a config file. In the cloud that breaks: instances are replaced on every deploy, added when traffic grows and removed when they crash, and each new one gets a new IP address. Service discovery is how callers find the current, healthy instances by name. Here Orders knows only the name 'payments' and needs a live lookup.
steps.idea: Instances come and go, so callers need a live lookup from a stable name to current addresses.
steps.caption: Orders knows a name, not any address.

steps.title: Instances announce themselves
steps.body: When an instance finishes starting and is ready for traffic, it tells the registry its service name and address, such as payments at 10.0.1.4:8080. The registry is a live phone book of who is available. Some systems have the instance register itself, and others have a platform agent do it. Register only when ready: an instance still loading its cache should not get traffic yet. In the animation, three Payments instances register.
steps.idea: A registry is a live map from a service name to the addresses that are ready right now.
steps.caption: Three Payments instances register.

steps.title: Staying registered means proving you are alive
steps.body: A crashed instance cannot say goodbye, so the registry needs another way to know. Each instance sends a heartbeat (a tiny 'I am alive' message) every 5 seconds. Or the registry checks a health endpoint instead. After 3 missed beats (15 seconds here, a typical choice) the entry is removed. On a clean shutdown, instances deregister first, so heartbeats are the safety net for crashes. Short intervals detect failure faster but add load, and can wrongly drop a healthy instance after a brief network blip (flapping).
steps.idea: Heartbeats plus a timeout turn silence into removal, so dead instances age out on their own.
steps.caption: Healthy instances keep sending heartbeats.

steps.title: The caller picks the instance
steps.body: In client-side discovery, Orders asks the registry for the list of healthy Payments addresses, keeps it in memory and picks one itself, for example round-robin (taking turns). In the animation it calls payments-2 directly, with no middle hop. The cost: every client, in every language, needs this lookup, caching and balancing code, and all of it must be kept up to date.
steps.idea: Client-side discovery saves a network hop but spreads discovery code into every caller.
steps.caption: Orders looks up the list, then calls payments-2 directly.

steps.title: A proxy picks for the caller
steps.body: In server-side discovery, Orders calls one stable address: a load balancer or proxy. The proxy keeps a fresh copy of the healthy list from the registry (it syncs in the background, not on every call), picks an instance and forwards the request. Callers stay simple and need no discovery code. The trade-off is an extra hop, often around 1 ms inside one data center, and the proxy itself must stay highly available.
steps.idea: Server-side discovery keeps callers simple but adds a hop and a component that must not fail.
steps.caption: Orders calls the load balancer, which routes to a healthy instance.

steps.title: Using DNS as the registry
steps.body: The simplest discovery tool is DNS. Payments gets a name such as payments.internal, and the platform keeps it pointing at the healthy addresses. A records give only IPs, so you need a fixed port or SRV records to learn the port. Every language already resolves names, so no client library is needed. The weakness is caching: an answer lives for its TTL (time to live, say 30 seconds). So a dead instance can stay in use for about 15 s (registry timeout) plus 30 s (TTL), roughly 45 s in the worst case.
steps.idea: DNS discovery works everywhere, but caching makes it slow to notice change.
steps.caption: DNS returns the current addresses, valid for the TTL.

steps.title: An instance dies
steps.body: Now payments-3 crashes without warning. It stops sending heartbeats, but the registry removes it only after 15 seconds, and a client with a cached list may keep it even longer. During that window about one call in three fails, because with 3 instances round-robin sends a third of the calls to the dead one. A retry on another instance hides most of this when the request never reached the dead one (a connect failure) or the call is idempotent. For a charge, send an idempotency key so a retry cannot bill twice.
steps.idea: Failure is never noticed instantly, so callers need timeouts and retries to cover the stale window.
steps.caption: Calls to the dead instance fail until it is removed.

steps.title: The registry itself is down
steps.body: By now payments-3 has been removed from the list. What if the registry itself becomes unreachable? A client that cached the last good list can keep calling instances, which is why caches are a feature, not a shortcut. New instances will not be found and dead ones will not be removed until the registry returns, but existing traffic keeps flowing. So registries run as replicated clusters, and callers keep serving from their last known list (serve stale) while retrying the registry in the background.
steps.idea: Run the registry as a cluster, and let callers keep serving from their last known list.
steps.caption: Orders keeps calling payments-2 from its cached list.

steps.title: Name in, healthy address out
steps.body: Instances register when ready and prove they are alive with heartbeats. Callers find them through the registry directly (client-side), through a proxy (server-side), or through DNS. Every approach has a delay between a failure and everyone noticing, so timeouts, retries and caches that survive a registry outage are part of the design. Kubernetes, for instance, gives each Service a stable DNS name and virtual IP, and routes only to pods that pass their readiness checks. Callers still need timeouts and retries.
steps.idea: Discovery maps names to healthy addresses. The real design work is handling stale answers.
steps.caption: Register, heartbeat, look up, call, retry.

quiz.q: A service sends heartbeats every 5 seconds and is removed after 3 missed beats. It crashes. About how long can the registry still list it?
options: Until someone deregisters it by hand
quiz.why: A crash gives no goodbye. The registry waits for 3 missed 5-second beats, so the dead entry can remain for up to roughly 15 seconds.

quiz.q: Your team uses five languages and wants no discovery code in callers and needs instant failover and load-aware routing. Which fits best, and what do you pay?
options: Client-side discovery; you pay with a stale cache
Server-side discovery; you pay an extra hop and must keep the proxy available
Heartbeats; you pay with longer TTLs
quiz.why: A proxy keeps logic out of every client, at the cost of one more hop and one more component that must stay highly available. DNS also avoids client code but adds TTL staleness.

quiz.q: Users report errors for about a minute after each deploy removes old instances, though DNS records update within seconds. What is the most likely cause?
options: The registry is storing too many instances
The load balancer has too many healthy backends
Clients cache DNS answers longer than the TTL, so they keep calling old addresses
quiz.why: Some runtimes cache DNS beyond the TTL, so they keep using addresses that no longer exist. Check resolver caching and add retries.

quiz.q: The registry goes down for two minutes. Orders cached the instance list 10 seconds ago. What should happen?
options: Orders keeps calling instances from its cached list
Orders stops calling Payments until the registry is back
Orders rebuilds the list using a broadcast
quiz.why: Existing traffic can continue from the last known list. Only changes, such as new or dead instances, go unnoticed until the registry returns.

cheatsheet.def: A store mapping a service name to the addresses of its currently healthy instances. Examples: Consul, etcd, Eureka, the Kubernetes API.
Instances report regularly; if reports stop for a set time, the entry is dropped. Shorter means faster detection but more load and false removals.
The caller queries the registry and picks an instance itself. No extra hop, but every client needs the logic.
The caller uses a stable proxy address, and the proxy looks up and picks an instance. Simpler clients, one extra hop.
A service name resolves to the current addresses. Works with every client, but TTLs and client caches delay updates.
Liveness asks whether the process is alive; readiness asks whether it can take traffic now. Register on readiness, restart on liveness.
The time between an instance failing and callers stopping use of it. Cover it with timeouts, retries and sensible TTLs.
